Question: Can lasers be used to defend against nuclear missiles or ballistic missiles?
Answer: In general, most missiles that will carry nuclear warheads are intermediate range of intercontinental range ballistic missiles. If they are launched from the center of the country (China or Russia or USA for examples), then there is no Earth based laser that is going to attach the launching missile. Once that missile reaches above the atmosphere (in general) the warheads separate from the missile body and are in very hard RVs (reentry vehicles) that are coming through the atmosphere Mach 25 or higher and are built to survive extreme thermal conditions. Therefore the laser will generally be useless in attacking a reentry vehicle as it is approaching a target in your country. HOWEVER, if the ballistic missiles are being launched from submarines, then it is possible for the defending country to position ships between the launching submarines and their country and use lasers to attack the rising missiles which are Much Easier to defeat. Whereas if the warheads are being carried by Cruise Missiles, then yes, the defending county could position land based lasers along possible ground tracks of cruise missiles and shoot down the missile or use an airborne laser to shoot down the cruise missile. There were plans for lasers on satellites orbiting the Earth and being used to attack launching ballistic missiles as they are high in the atmosphere over their country, or to attack high altitude bombers that may carry nuclear bombs or cruise missiles. All of those options are continually being evaluated and the USA is spending a Lot of effort and money to develop solid-state lasers to use on the global battlefield.

There are 60 nautical miles per degree of Latitude or one nautical mile is a minute of Latitude. 90 degrees or 5400 minutes does not divide evenly into meters or kilometers. The English system (or British system) of units is “human based” or human friendly. Pounds versus kilograms. Question: What types of commercial airliners have a tail-mounted engine? Are there any that do not have one, and if so, why?
Answer: Tail mounted. That means attached to the vertical tail (stabilizer) as opposed to being attached to the aft section of the fuselage. The primary tail mounted aircraft had an Odd number of engines (three) in order to be able to meet the requirements (at the time) for reliability and safety flying over the Earth’s oceans. For example, the Boeing 727 was a smaller single-aisle aircraft that could fly from mainland USA (example) to various islands and with a single-engine (of the three) not working, could make it to an airport for an emergency landing. Then when the larger twin-aisle aircraft were designed, there was the behemoth Boeing 747 with four engines, and the Douglas DC-10 and the Lockheed L-1011 both with three engines all competing to carry lots of passengers over long ranges and therefore had to meet the single engine out (of three or four) while over the oceans. Douglas DC-10 or McDonnell-Douglas DC-10 (depending upon what year) and the Lockheed L-1011 There are a Lot of structural issues with placing an engine on the vertical tail (tail-mounted) and when the engines became much more reliable you have the Boeing 777 carrying a lot of passengers with only Two LARGE very-reliable engines Three engines to meet the FAA and EASA requirements for having one engine out over the ocean and being able to divert to land at an airport in an emergency. At the time they needed three engines because of the thrust to weight ratio at the time. Simple and logical.

Question: Why do people who complain about diversity hiring think that candidates are hired for simply being black or brown when they would never be considered if they didn't have the qualifications in the first place.?
Answer: Because, unfortunately, that is not how DEI is looked at in the USA. I would want DEI to be used to train recruiters to “beat the bushes” to get the best qualified people of All types to apply for jobs or apply to enter college, etc. But unfortunately that is not the primary tactic. Instead the general public is constantly bombarded that “this college or industry or employer or board of directors etc.” only has a small percentage of “this race or that ethnicity or that gender” and therefore is bad. No one checks to see what the “pool of applicants” consists of. Instead of DEI, the USA should FOCUS on pre-K and elementary school education be available (for FREE) to ALL and to be equally as good all over the place so that every child, starting at age 2 or 3, has a nearly equal chance to learn and succeed and then apply for those colleges or those jobs. Then there would be No need for DEI at all, because the applicant pool would always be equally balanced based on the percentage of those “types of people” in the US population. But that takes time, and some people want to artificially fill the ranks today. MIT did it in the late 1960’s (when I was applying to be a freshman), by searching high and wide for “gems in the rough”, admitting them and providing them 6 weeks of intense pre-college initiation prior to the start of freshman year. Therefore, I had a lot of black, Hispanic and female classmates which was Great, as they all were great. Then I as a male assisted the admissions department for several years in the late 1970’s to go to high schools around my area with other male and female MIT alumni and speak with all the high school freshman girls and tell them there were Many future jobs for females in STEM careers and that males liked females in STEM careers. Within, a dozen years of that the percentage of undergraduate females at MIT went from 15% to 48%. THAT is how you do Diversity, by stimulating a Diverse set of people to Apply. Simple and logical. Unfortunately, DEI became a governing “religion” in many places across the USA and it was Not right and it is time to start with the 2 to 10 year olds, give them ALL a Good and Equal education and then let the number of applicants to college and jobs play out over time.

Question: Is it possible to get into a top university without playing sports, even if you were involved in clubs?

Question: What are the best possible ways to study (for middle school, high school and college)?
Answer: In college, living on campus 24x7, it is relatively easy to form study groups to assist your learning and understanding for some of the harder courses. You are still submitting your own work (home work assignments and projects) but you cross-learn with other students. In high school that also can work, by getting on your cell phone with a video app and working together with one or two others to assist each other in learning the “hard-stuff” but still only submitting your work. Middle school is a place to learn how to work in groups and take advantage of the resources of the school about you on your own. You can do something similar to what one would do in high school, as middle school is to Prepare you to undertake high school as an individual. Always remember that there are 168 hours in every week and slightly more than 52 weeks in each year. You don’t have to do Everything every day. Some things can be done on weekends or during school vacations. However, you MUST have excellent time management to allow you the proper distribution of time to properly do home work and course projects. 10 hours spread over 8 days is much better than 10 hours over night before an assignment is due or a test is scheduled. Become a Master of Time Management and learn to form supportive study groups and you will succeed in life.

Question: Do you have to start over when transferring colleges?
Answer: Why would you think that???? When you transfer colleges, you are expected to transfer Credits. Now, if you are expected to get 30 credits per academic year (120 total) to graduate and you transfer from College A to College B having completed 30 credits at College A, then College B may not give you credit for all 30, and instead give you credit for 15 units towards graduation and allow the other 15 to be “extra”. Then you either spend another academic term at College B to earn your bachelors degree or you take some courses that satisfy College B during some of the summers. For example, not to transfer but to get ahead in math, I took a differential equations course taught by Syracuse University during the summer after freshman year near my home, and MIT accepted it, counted the credit and allowed me to start Advanced Calculus. That allowed me the ability to do a Co-Op during the 2nd term junior year because I could still graduate on time. You apply to transfer and your official transcript is submitted by the first college to the second college as part of the application process. The admissions committee rules first, but then each department rules on whether the credits you have meet the minimum standard at that college for that course. I had to show the text book and answer questions from the head of the MIT math department to get the credit for the course I mentioned, above. When you transfer into a top college like MIT (example) you may enter after your sophomore year at your first college, but you may have to repeat your sophomore year at MIT. Whereas at many public colleges you may not lose any of the credits that you earned at the first college. Good luck.

Question: What is Title IX, and how does it impact you as a student?
Answer: I started at MIT in the Fall of 1969, several years Prior to Title IX being passed to require equality of female students with male students when it comes to all college activities, if the college accepts any Federal Funding. However, my high school already had more sports for females than males (about 50/50 split for students) and MIT had more sports for females (based on the number of females vs males). So it never impacted my high school district (upstate NY) or MIT. The number of MIT female students continued to increase (roughly 50/50 by late 1990’s) and the sports are all balanced. Title IX was mostly for the majority of colleges and high schools that were ignorant of the Fact that females can play and enjoy playing sports just as much if not more than the males. Simple and logical. Later in the 1970’s as a MIT graduate student I coached a co-ed JV soccer team until there were enough female players to start their own team, I helped to start the Wellesley College varsity soccer team, and I assisted the MIT women in starting their own ice hockey team. Wonderful!!! HOWEVER: There is a downside to Title IX. There are (I believe) three ways to determine whether a college/school is in Title IX compliance and most choose only one of those ways. In that manner, wrestling, volleyball, and gymnastics have been horribly Diminished (across all colleges) for males. Also, instead of allowing women to play football the colleges propped up field hockey, and they created a weird version of Lacrosse when it is not really Lacrosse for the women. But, since they are in “compliance” they don’t care.

Question: Can I pursue a second bachelor’s degree again?
Answer: Let’s think this through. In general, a college expects an undergraduate student to take roughly 5 courses per term or 10 courses per academic year for four years or 40 courses in order to earn a bachelors degree. Typically, some one only needs 10 to 11 courses beyond that to earn a Masters degree in your niche area. Obviously, that assumes you have a bachelors degree supporting that niche area. If you don’t have a bachelors degree in that niche area, then you will have to take some undergraduate courses to get the prerequisites required for those graduate level courses in your niche area. For example, a colleague of mine majored in Applied Physics and wanted a masters in Aero-Astro Engineering. MIT required him to take 9 undergraduate Aero-Astro courses over one year (at his expense) and then his fully-funded graduate degree program kicked-in over the following two years including his thesis work, and he was awarded a Masters degree. A second bachelors degree would have been “Stupid”, at his own expense and he still wouldn’t get what he wanted: Advanced training in a niche area of real interest to him in Aero-Astro Engineering. So, he took roughly 40 courses for his bachelors degree, and then ~20 courses for his Masters degree. Whereas if a college admits you for a second bachelors degree (and many will NOT), then you would have to petition to get out of taking 80 courses to get those two degrees…… Given the cost of a single bachelors degree that would be Stupid and Horribly expensive. So either get a Dual degree in the 4 to 5 years of your college work at the same college, and probably only need ~50 courses to get the two degrees, and if you are at an elite private US college, you may pay Nothing more or very little more to do that…….. EXAMPLE: Get your bachelors degree in Engineering (for example) and then later go to a public college in your area and sign-up to be a history major, and depending upon what you already took for your engineering distribution requirements (I took history and political science and some economics courses), you may only need, ~8 undergraduate history courses then followed by 11 masters level courses, and instead of having two bachelors degrees you will have a bachelors of engineering and a masters in history. Nice, and a Lot cheaper and faster. Simple and logical.

Question: What is Spin Launch? Will they be able to defeat the rocket equation?
Answer: Spin launch: and First, there is the qualifying statement: “Any equipment or goods delivered by SpinLaunch must be capable of withstanding up to 10,000 G's of force for 30 minutes during the centrifugal acceleration process. Additionally, no more than 880 lb (400 kg) of payload can be sent per launch” The delivery system used by spin launch exits the centrifuge at high speed and with NO THRUST. The only forces acting on the “rocket” is gravity and aerodynamic drag until it reaches an altitude of ~200,000 feet and starts its rocket motor. Thus, knowing the Coefficient of Drag (and the area over which to apply the drag) as a function of Mach number you can calculate the velocity it will have when it reaches 200,000 feet (and, of course, the velocity by which it must exit the centrifuge in order to reach 200 kFt). I have an Excel workbook that will solve this for you. If you know the starting mass, the area over which the drag is being applied and the coefficient of drag as a function of Mach number, and have an excellent database (part of the workbook) for the properties of the Earth’s atmosphere to 500 kFT, you can calculate all of the parameters required to get your payload to orbital velocity. You can then vary the parameters, including the starting altitude of the centrifuge above sea level and solve for an optimum set-up for the centrifuge as designed by Spin Launch. Simple. Good luck and enjoy the calculations.

Question: What is the purpose of issuing grades in middle school? This is a serious question and I would love some input from educators. I am a student, it stems from a conversation, and I am trying to gain perspective.

Question: What are the benefits of joining the military for culinary school?
Answer: The other answers are great and for the modern times. Here is an anecdote: During World War 2 my father was the lead officer of a mobile radar unit in the US Army from late 1942 until June of 1945. Towards the beginning of his command when they were in Northern Africa (prior to the invasion of Sicily and then fighting through Italy into Belgium and the Netherlands) he had a meeting with his master sergeant. “The soldiers are complaining about the food and our trucks are continually breaking down, call in the lead cook and the head of maintenance and lets figure out how to solve these issues” The head of maintenance came in and they spoke for several minutes, and then my Dad asked him: “What did you do in civilian life before you were drafted?” The soldier replied: “Sir, I was the head chef at the Waldorf Astoria in NY City”…….. Then they brought in the head cook. After a couple of minutes of discussion, my father asked the same question and the reply: “Sir, I was the head mechanic for a major trucking company” The US Army, when they drafted, didn’t always check to see where to assign the entering soldiers, but placed them into the open billets. My father then switched the roles of the two soldiers, never telling the upper commanders, and there were no more complaints about food nor maintenance for the next ~three years. There were complaints about getting shot-at in the front lines or going behind enemy lines to capture enemy radar systems…….

The Soviet Union had aircraft carrier fleets for a number of years, but when the Soviet Union broke up, Russia did not need aircraft carriers to project power. They can project power around their Huge borders with land based aircraft and do so all the time. Thus you have aircraft carrier fleets to protect valuable trading routes across the ocean, to protect allies and to “project power” where you believe it assists your country (cost-effective). Question: What is the importance of academic freedom in US universities and why do they have the ability to hire and fire faculty members at their discretion? How does this differ from other countries?
Answer: The departments of the various US colleges have the ability to hire the professors that they wish to have or at least wish to “try out”. Most will start in an Untenured position, as an assistant or possibly as an associate professor. When they are hired the process of obtaining tenure is explained to them. Then after the pre-stated period of time (when they were hired) the untenured professors are reviewed by the tenure board of that department or school (for example, the School of Engineering at MIT will review tenure for engineering professors in the various engineering departments). During the tenure review the person will be evaluated on research, publications, bringing-in research funds and teaching. If they fail the tenure review they may be given another shorter period of time to try and correct their short-comings and will get typically one more chance at passing the tenure review. Once they pass the tenure review, they are tenured and guaranteed a position at the college as long as they don’t do anything Illegal (general public) and possibly some other obvious restrictions that were well-spelled out to all of the professors. A tenured professor can’t be fired, but it may be possible to be “let go” if the department fails to obtain sufficient funding and the department is eliminated, unless the tenured professor is accepted in another department. Not certain how this differs from other countries. In the USA, a tenured professor can’t be “fired” if they are doing the research, teaching and bringing-in research that they are expected to do. Thus they can make “political statements” (for example) and not be fired. That is part of the foundation of academic freedom. And they can work on Any funded-research no matter if others don’t like the subject matter, as long as the research is generally considered legal. So hire/fire at the department’s discretion is only at the Beginning. Once the college has granted tenure to the professor, they can’t be fired except for some gross acts that would be delineated for years for all to know about.

Many very good students get financial aid (grants and/or scholarships) from the colleges. Indeed, any US state that claims two years of free tuition at a state public college actually means they expect that $6,500 from the Federal government each year….. And most public in-state 4-year colleges cost ~$13,000 in annual tuition/fees so half is paid by the Feds. Skin in the Game. The ADULT student should be investing in themselves. That is the Capitalist way of doing things and that is the USA.

Question: Is there any advice about entering America for a 6 month trip I should know? I’ve just graduated high school, from the UK, and want to travel around California before going to Uni. I have my b1 visa but I know US border control can be quite intense
Answer: First unless you got your visa to conduct Business in the USA you don’t have a B-1 visa but a B-2 visa for tourism: Second, you get the visa from the US Department of State. However, when you enter the USA you must pass through and be interviewed by the Customs and Border Patrol agents who work for a Different US agency (Department of Homeland Security) and they can REJECT you and place you on the Next flight that is headed out of the USA and generally towards the UK. Therefore, take their questions Seriously. If they even suspect that you are entering the USA on the B-2 visa in order to stay in the USA illegally, then they will not let you enter and send you away. Pack clothing and items that are typically expected for a tourist and don’t show up with so many belongings that it looks like you are moving to the USA. Relax and answer the specific questions naturally and you should be OK. Good luck.
